reason: Both pages get the numbers right against facts.md: 14 of 72, the 58/72 escalation split, break-evens of 0.11 cents and 13.3 cents, and $405/$500/$662 at 5 cents for 10,000 invoices. They also stay right when price and volume change; at 50 cents and 200,000 invoices A shows $80,599/$85,736 and B at $0.25 shows $40,324/$45,460/$199,279/$166,300. A wins on how it reads on a phone. Steps 1-2 animate real invoices test-012 and test-002 through the ask-twice gate. Step 3 sorts 72 dots into 14 accepted and 58 sent on. Step 4 shows the break-even sum ($2.18 / 1,944 and $259 / 1,944). Steps 5-6 let the reader sweep the price and the volume on a chart that is legible at 390 px, and step 7 ends with the two thresholds and stated uncertainty (72/72 is still consistent with a success rate as low as 94.9%). B has more material: a three-route intro, a 72-square grid you can tap for each invoice, price chips that jump to each break-even, and the cheap-alone and person-review comparisons. But its step 5 card, the key break-even step, overflows at 390 px and cuts off the title, text, button and stat tiles on the right. Its savings chart text is also too small to read on a phone.

A: The 'No check' label means 'expensive model on every invoice', which a newcomer could read as 'cheap model alone'.
The Claude reviewer check first appears in step 2 with no explanation of what it is or that it is a stronger paid model.
Fixed-height card leaves large empty gaps on steps 1-4 and 7, and the step 3 'wrong answer' legend has no red dots in its final state.
B: The step 5 card ('Does the saving cover the cost of checking?') overflows horizontally at 390 px and clips the heading, body text, the 'Try a price' button and the third stat tile.
Axis labels, break-even labels and line names on the monthly saving chart are about 6-7 px at phone width and hard to read.
It is a long scroll: the stepper's Next button sits above the invoice grid it changes, so on a phone each step's visual is below the fold from the controls.
